newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai markets seen nervous despite new finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Thai markets seen nervous despite new finance minister.

text.p: Thailand's ailing markets will gyrate nervously this week, despite the naming of a new finance minister, amid concerns about banks' loan portfolios and uncertainty about the embattled baht, analysts said.

Friday's appointment of banker Thanong Bidaya to replace the respected Amnuay Viravan was received cautiously by the battered stock market, now at eight-year lows, but the baht failed to light up on the news.

Analysts said investors remained spooked by the poor quality of loans, worth billions of dollars, made by the troubled financial sector to cash-strapped property firms. As a result bank stocks were expected to be sold further.
"I expect the stock market to move in a narrow range with signs the index could fall slightly," said Payuha Boonsiri at Nithipat Capital.
On Friday the SET index ended up 15.48 points at 480.25 after eight straight days of losses.

Analysts said other concerns are the poor state of some weaker finance firms, among the more than 90 in the country, and the continued absence of an official framework to encourage consolidations and mergers in the ailing sector, they added.
Last month, a much-touted merger between Thai Danu Bank Plc and Finance One Plc, Thailand's biggest finance firm, collapsed after tax and legal complications.

The government then promised to announce more flexible merger rules but so far nothing has been announced, and analysts said the fear now was that authorities might just let the weaker and smaller institutions sink.
Another pressure was anticipation in the offshore market of a baht devaluation and uncertainty about government policy to manage the currency, they said.
The baht came under speculative attack last month, forcing the central bank to impose currency controls which cut off baht supplies from local sources to foreign speculators.

"It (the appointment of new finance minister) is relatively a non-factor. I don't think his appointment will help regain market confidence in the economy," said Satit Wannasilpin at Capital Nomura Securities Plc.

The low-profile Thanong, president of Thai Military Bank, replaced Amnuay who quit after differences with political rivals in the six-party coalition government of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.

Two polls published on Sunday by the respected Suan Dusit Rajabhat Institute and the privately run Assumption University gave Thanong a weak rating. He was ranked ninth out of 10 and 11 choices, respectively, in the polls which were conducted separately.
Chavalit told a news conference on Sunday that Thanong needed time in order to carry out his duties effectively.

Last week, the assistant governor of the central Bank of Thailand, Siri Ganjarerndeem, said there was no need for the market to worry about a devaluation of the baht. But some foreign analysts believe that devaluation has become virtually inevitable.
"The longer they leave it the worse it gets," said Daniel Hemmant, currency fund manager at Guinness Flight Asia Ltd.

But other analysts said the chances of an outright devaluation were remote, although the central bank could consider a more flexible trading band for the baht or adjust the trade-weighted basket it is pegged to. At present the basket is dominated by the dollar.

"Interest rates need to go down, and at some point there needs to be flexibility on the baht trading band and the composition of the basket of currencies it is pegged to," said Graham Catterwell, managing director of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
